chapter: King Oliver's band and early jazz
title: Tom Anderson's, Albert Nicholas leaving, and the call from Oliver
summary: Oliver had not known him; Bigard was laid off at Tom Anderson's when Albert Nicholas quietly left for Chicago, the boss begged him back with a $10 raise to $35, and Luis Russell later had Joe send for him.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Had you known Joe Oliver in New

No. Oh, they were before my time. Well, he heard about me through -- Luis Russell left the band and he went to join King Oliver in Chicago. And then, the funny part, when I got to Chicago -- you see, Albert Nicholas went to Chicago. He left the group. We was working at Tom Anderson's for quite a while, just he and I, a duet, and the trumpet and -- but he didn't tell the man -- he was a Sneaky Pete -- he didn't tell the man he was going to leave, you know, because the man's business turned to bad and the man had to leave one of the musicians go. And I was the last one to join the group so they decided that it would be better for me, being the last one to come into the group, to be laid off.

So I got laid off. And the week I got laid off, that's when Albert took off for Chicago. So he left, and the boss was so angry that he didn't tell him that he was going to leave because he would never have fired me, you know. So he told the guys to go to my house and tell me to come back to work. I said, "I wouldn't come back to work for nothing in the world." So the guys told him I wouldn't come back to work.

So he came to my house himself and begged me to come back. I said, "No, I won't come back." He said, "I'll give you a raise." So he gave me a raise, gave me a $10 raise to come back. I said, "Okay," and I went back to work.
How much were you making then?
$25 a week. So I was making '35 a week, then, see? And that was big money in those days, you know. But our tips -- we had a kitty, and we was doing all right.
But Albert did dirty, you see. He was sneaky. He wouldn't tell the man, he said, "Well, I'm going to Chicago. Don't fire him." I don't know, he didn't tell the man that.
And then a little later on Luis Russell had Joe send for me. That's what he did.
